main.title: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl
main.summary: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl (titled S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chornobyl on consoles) is a first-person shooter video game developed by GSC Game World and published by THQ in 2007 following a long development.

cards.heading: A second disaster in the Zone
cards.text: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl (titled S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chornobyl on consoles) is a first-person shooter video game developed by GSC Game World and published by THQ in 2007 following a long development. It is the first game in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchise, set in an alternate reality where a second disaster of mysterious origin occurred at the Chernobyl exclusion zone, which further contaminated the surrounding area with radiation, and caused strange otherworldly changes in local fauna, flora, and the laws of physics. The background and some of the terminology of the game are borrowed from the 1971 novella Roadside Picnic and its 1979 film adaptation Stalker.

cards.heading: The Marked One searches for Strelok
cards.text: The game features a non-linear storyline with 7 different endings and includes role-playing gameplay elements such as trading and two-way communication with non-player characters. In the game, the player assumes the identity of the Marked One, an amnesiac man trying to find and kill the mysterious Strelok within the exclusion zone, a forbidden territory surrounding the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.

cards.heading: Atmosphere, bugs and a continuing series
cards.text: The game was met with praise for the atmosphere, style and depth, as well as the level design, but was criticized for numerous bugs. It was also a commercial success, selling over 2 million copies by September of 2008. A prequel, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, was released in 2008. A sequel, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat, followed in 2009. A second sequel, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl, was released in 2024. There are also multiple fan remakes trying to restore the cut content from the original version of the game.

main.title: Jetpac Refuelled
main.subtitle: Assemble the rocket before leaving the planet
main.summary: Jetpac Refuelled is Rare's Xbox Live Arcade shooting game, released on 28 March 2007. It rebuilds the central idea of the 1983 Jetpac with a larger set of stages and a new high-definition presentation. Jetman collects the parts of a rocket, carries fuel to it and tries to escape while hostile creatures move around the screen. Flying makes the collection straightforward to understand, but carrying something gives the player another responsibility. The rocket is both the objective and the place repeatedly returned to, turning each level into a series of dangerous deliveries.

cards.heading: Assemble the rocket before leaving the planet
cards.text: Jetpac Refuelled is Rare's Xbox Live Arcade shooting game, released on 28 March 2007. It rebuilds the central idea of the 1983 Jetpac with a larger set of stages and a new high-definition presentation. Jetman collects the parts of a rocket, carries fuel to it and tries to escape while hostile creatures move around the screen. Flying makes the collection straightforward to understand, but carrying something gives the player another responsibility. The rocket is both the objective and the place repeatedly returned to, turning each level into a series of dangerous deliveries.

cards.heading: Make room for the next fuel canister
cards.text: The playfield wraps horizontally, offering a route around threats rather than forcing every approach through the centre. Platforms provide resting places while the jetpack allows rapid changes in height. Shooting clears a temporary path, but enemies keep the surroundings active as the next item falls into view. Gold and other resources add optional rewards beside the immediate launch preparations. The player decides when a detour is worth the danger and when the sensible move is to complete the rocket. A small collection of actions creates competing demands within a single screen.

cards.heading: An older Rare idea in a new digital library
cards.text: Refuelled expands the formula to 128 stages, with online competition, rankings and achievements linking it to Xbox Live Arcade. Steve Burke composed the music. Rare sought to retain the original's recognisable activity while giving the return enough visual and mechanical change to stand as its own game. Reviews generally welcomed the update while questioning repetition and aspects of multiplayer. It later joined Rare Replay in 2015. The game connects two periods of the studio's history through a particularly clear task: gather the rocket, refuel it and survive long enough to reach somewhere else.

main.title: Final Fantasy XII: Revenant Wings
main.subtitle: Vaan takes command in the sky
main.summary: Final Fantasy XII: Revenant Wings is Think & Feel and Square Enix's Nintendo DS strategy adventure following Vaan and Penelo after their earlier journey. Their life as sky pirates leads them into a conflict around the floating continent of Lemurés. The player commands groups of summoned creatures in real time, giving the familiar characters a different role on the battlefield. An airship connects destinations and missions. The world of Ivalice returns through a smaller machine, but the central task is now directing a force rather than controlling one fighter's immediate actions.

cards.heading: Vaan takes command in the sky
cards.text: Final Fantasy XII: Revenant Wings is Think & Feel and Square Enix's Nintendo DS strategy adventure following Vaan and Penelo after their earlier journey. Their life as sky pirates leads them into a conflict around the floating continent of Lemurés. The player commands groups of summoned creatures in real time, giving the familiar characters a different role on the battlefield. An airship connects destinations and missions. The world of Ivalice returns through a smaller machine, but the central task is now directing a force rather than controlling one fighter's immediate actions.

cards.heading: Orders drawn with a stylus
cards.text: Commanders lead squads across mission maps, and the touchscreen makes selecting a group and directing its movement a physical gesture. Different objectives give the force something more specific to do than simply clear every opponent. The summoned creatures provide the units through which those orders take effect. A useful plan depends on bringing the appropriate group to the right place while the battle continues. The handheld format makes this a compact interpretation of real-time strategy, with the player watching several small actions develop from a sequence of direct orders.

cards.heading: A base between the islands
cards.text: The airship gradually becomes more than a way to choose the next destination. Shops provide equipment and materials, while an artificer can turn resources collected during missions into useful items. Preparation therefore returns to a shared place between encounters. Much of the music arranges Hitoshi Sakimoto's Final Fantasy XII score, with new pieces by Kenichiro Fukui linking the change of genre to the earlier adventure. Revenant Wings gives its continuation a distinct purpose: familiar people and sounds support a new way of organising action in Ivalice.

main.title: Moero! Nekketsu Rhythm Damashii: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan 2
main.subtitle: Another squad across the town
main.summary: Moero! Nekketsu Rhythm Damashii: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan 2 is iNiS's Nintendo DS sequel about musical encouragement. The returning cheer squad from Yuuhi Town now shares its world with a rival group from Asahi Town, whose blue uniforms distinguish them from the original team's black jackets. Both answer people who shout for help when their troubles become overwhelming. The separate stories range from everyday anxieties to extravagant emergencies. Their common solution is still a performance in which the player supplies the timing that keeps the cheering alive.

cards.heading: Another squad across the town
cards.text: Moero! Nekketsu Rhythm Damashii: Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan 2 is iNiS's Nintendo DS sequel about musical encouragement. The returning cheer squad from Yuuhi Town now shares its world with a rival group from Asahi Town, whose blue uniforms distinguish them from the original team's black jackets. Both answer people who shout for help when their troubles become overwhelming. The separate stories range from everyday anxieties to extravagant emergencies. Their common solution is still a performance in which the player supplies the timing that keeps the cheering alive.

cards.heading: Two teams share the same beat
cards.text: The touchscreen continues to carry the numbered targets, traced phrases and spinning markers, while the upper screen follows the person being encouraged. Accuracy sustains the spirit meter and changes how well that person's efforts are going. The new squad expands the cast without requiring another control scheme: both groups use the same gestures. The contrast is in their appearance and the situations they enter. That consistency lets the sequel introduce another community of characters while keeping the player's attention on listening and performing a particular song.

cards.heading: An opportunity to try again
cards.text: A failed performance can be reviewed through its final few seconds, helping the player recognise the passage that caused trouble before attempting it again. The feature suits a game whose hardest moments often depend on one brief change in rhythm. Returning characters also appear across different stories, giving the episodes a sense of shared neighbourhoods. The rivalry eventually becomes cooperation on a larger scale. The sequel keeps its musical challenges demanding while surrounding repeated attempts with a world in which encouragement is always worth another try.

main.title: Odin Sphere
main.summary: Odin Sphere is an action role-playing game developed by Vanillaware for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Odin Sphere is an action role-playing game developed by Vanillaware for the PlayStation 2. It was published by Atlus (Japan and North America) in 2007, and by Square Enix (Australia and Europe) in 2008. A remake, titled Odin Sphere Leifthrasir, was released on PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, and PlayStation Vita in 2016: Atlus handled publishing duties in Japan and North America, while NIS America published the title in PAL territories.

Using a two-dimensional side-scrolling perspective, gameplay focuses on a beat em up-style fighting system while incorporating role-playing elements — Leifthrasir expands upon and refines these elements. The story, shared between both versions, follows five characters on the fantasy continent of Erion during a war between the nations of Ragnanival and Ringford over a weapon called the Crystallization Cauldron, and their roles in the Armageddon, a catastrophe which will destroy Erion.

The game was conceived by George Kamitani as first a sequel and then a spiritual successor to the 1997 Sega Saturn title Princess Crown. Development began in 2004 after the official formation of Vanillaware. The story was based around the concept of a Valkyrie princess. The scenario and world design incorporated Norse mythology, the works of William Shakespeare, fairy tales and early video games. 2D graphics were chosen over 3D graphics as Kamitani felt the style was stagnating, which necessitated presenting cutscenes as if on a stage rather than using traditional cinematography. Leifthrasir began development in 2013 as a means of addressing the issues both players and staff had with the original game while keeping the story intact. The music for both versions was composed by a team from Basiscape, led by company founder Hitoshi Sakimoto.

Prior to Atlus picking up the title, Vanillaware had encountered difficulties finding a publisher due to Kamitani's sparse record as a developer. Completed in 2006, Odin Sphere was delayed into the following year so it would not compete with Atlus' own titles. The localization was handled by Atlus USA, and proved challenging in multiple areas. Upon release, it garnered a positive reception from video game journalists: praise was given to its story, visuals and old-school gameplay, with criticism focused on its inventory system and framerate issues. Leifthrasir was praised for its improved performance and reworked mechanics. The game was a commercial success, contributing to the rise of Vanillaware as a developer.

main.title: Mario Party 8
main.subtitle: The carnival reaches the Wii Remote
main.summary: Mario Party 8 is Hudson Soft's Wii debut for the party series, released in North America on 29 May 2007.

cards.heading: The carnival reaches the Wii Remote
cards.text: Mario Party 8 is Hudson Soft's Wii debut for the party series, released in North America on 29 May 2007. MC Ballyhoo and his talking hat host a carnival of boards and minigames. Four competitors collect Stars while movement, items and events change their fortunes between the short challenges. The Wii Remote gives the gathering another physical vocabulary, making a minigame's instruction something the player may answer with a swing, a point or a tilt as well as a conventional button press.

cards.heading: A small gesture becomes the next challenge
cards.text: The six boards provide different settings for the race, while the Party Tent offers free-for-all, paired and one-on-one arrangements. The player still needs to consider the next Star and the items that can help reach it, but the minigames change how success is demonstrated. Moving between ordinary board turns and gesture-based tasks lets the controller support both a familiar strategic rhythm and an immediately visible action. The group can watch another person's movement in the room as well as the character's response on screen.

cards.heading: A familiar board with a different controller
cards.text: Separate areas collect minigame challenges, extra activities and unlockable rewards, with some games allowing the use of Miis. Star Battle Arena provides a one-on-one progression across the boards for a solo player. Carnival cards purchase further content, including music and character voices, while Yoshihiro Tsukahara's score supports the festive setting. Mario Party 8 carries the series into Wii's broader social approach to control, keeping its board-game foundation while making the next short challenge an opportunity to pass around a different kind of controller.

main.title: Forza Motorsport 2
main.summary: Forza Motorsport 2 is a 2007 simulation racing video game developed by Turn 10 Studios for the Xbox 360 console.

cards.heading: Forza reaches Xbox 360
cards.text: Forza Motorsport 2 is a 2007 simulation racing video game developed by Turn 10 Studios for the Xbox 360 console. It is the second title in the Forza series, and is the sequel to the original Forza Motorsport (2005) and was followed by Forza Motorsport 3 (2009).

cards.heading: Career and multiplayer racing
cards.text: Forza Motorsport 2 is a simulation racing video game on the Xbox 360 and the sequel to Forza Motorsport, which was released for the Xbox in 2005. Players compete in events around the globe using real licensed cars on a variety of real-world and fictional courses. It features an arcade mode, meant more for quickplay of races, and a career mode, which is focused on long-term play. Career mode spans several racing disciplines. Players can drive anything from common commuter cars to rare and expensive cars such as the Super GT and Deutsche Tourenwagen Masters vehicles. The game supports split-screen, System Link and Xbox Live multiplayer gaming. Split-screen allows two-player head-to-head racing, while both System Link and Xbox Live allow up to eight players to participate in a single race. Using Xbox Live, players can also buy in-game cars through the game's auction house, sell and 'gift' cars.

cards.heading: Cars and the livery editor
cards.text: The livery editor expands from the original game's 600 graphic layers to 4,000, letting players combine shapes, letters and pictures into detailed paint schemes. Designs can be sold through online auctions. Including downloadable content, the game offers 349 cars divided into production and racing classes; a car's class determines which events it can enter.

cards.heading: Racing on circuits
cards.text: Forza Motorsport 2 concentrates on circuit racing; point to point races which were featured in the original Forza Motorsport have been removed. Real world tracks Road Atlanta, Silverstone, Laguna Seca, Tsukuba, Mugello Circuit, Sebring International Raceway, Suzuka Circuit, and Nürburgring Nordschleife are licensed and included. Forza 2 is also one of the first racing games to prominently feature cars from the American Le Mans Series in both the game and downloadable content.

cards.heading: Damage and online car ownership
cards.text: Damage settings range from cosmetic effects to simulation damage severe enough to disable a car. Players can inspect the condition of individual parts through an on-screen display. Xbox Live also supports leaderboards, tournaments and an auction house where a purchased car retains details such as mileage, repair costs and previous owners. A photo mode lets players share images through the game's website.

cards.heading: A wheel developed with the game
cards.text: Microsoft developed the Xbox 360 Wireless Racing Wheel alongside Forza Motorsport 2, with professional racing drivers contributing to testing. The wheel supplies force feedback during play. Racing runs at 60 frames per second at 720p, while menus and replays run at 30 frames per second; replays use additional visual effects.

cards.heading: Recording the cars
cards.text: The Forza Motorsport 2 audio team set out to create a more realistic soundtrack that improves gameplay, immerses the player, and changes with car customization. They recorded actual cars on dynos with an array of microphones. To implement the audio, they matched the sample loops to engine speeds and used DSP techniques to enhance the sound. Additional recording was done on turbochargers, superchargers, straight-cut gears, tires, and collisions.

main.title: Tomb Raider: Anniversary
main.subtitle: Lara returns to the first adventure
main.summary: On June 1, 2007 Crystal Dynamics returned Lara Croft to the ruins of the first Tomb Raider, using the movement, physics and direction developed after Legend.

cards.heading: Revisiting the original Tomb Raider
cards.text: Crystal Dynamics released Tomb Raider: Anniversary on June 1, 2007. It revisits the locations and encounters of the 1996 original using the movement and physics developed for Tomb Raider: Legend. Familiar ruins become new climbing and puzzle spaces for Lara's expanded range of moves.

cards.heading: Ledges, grappling hooks and traversal
cards.text: Tomb Raider: Anniversary is a single-player action-adventure game where the player controls the protagonist, Lara Croft, from a third-person perspective, through fourteen levels set across four locations around the world. Lara can jump, climb and shimmy along ledges and vertical poles or ladders, crawl through small spaces, and swing on ropes and horizontal poles. Other abilities include interacting with objects and switches, using a grappling hook to latch onto special rings for both puzzle solving and environmental traversal, and swim and dive underwater for a limited time. Different button combinations can create more moves such as a roll and swan dive.

cards.heading: Switches, keys and timed puzzles
cards.text: Puzzles block progress through the levels until Lara solves them by activating switches or finding and using keys hidden within the area. These involve avoiding traps and timed environmental elements. In some sections, the player must pass quick time events by reacting to control prompts that appear on screen. While exploring, Lara can find large and small Medipacks that can heal damage suffered during gameplay, items which allow progress through a level or the larger game, and hidden artefacts and relics which unlock rewards such as costumes once collected. Once completed, a time trial is unlocked for each level, with further bonus features unlocking once the time trial is completed successfully.

cards.heading: Dodging a charge and counterattacking
cards.text: Lara can keep firing at a locked target while moving to avoid its attacks. Repeated shots enrage tougher enemies and draw them into a charge. As they close, time slows, offering a dodge and a carefully timed head shot when the reticles meet. The attack can kill an ordinary enemy or heavily damage a boss. Her twin pistols never run out of ammunition, while the shotgun, heavier handguns and miniature submachine guns require collected supplies. Choosing a weapon therefore balances immediate power against what may be needed after the next checkpoint.

main.title: Crossfire
main.summary: Crossfire (Korean: 크로스파이어) is an online tactical first-person shooter game developed by Smilegate Entertainment for Microsoft Windows.

cards.text: Crossfire (Korean: 크로스파이어) is an online tactical first-person shooter game developed by Smilegate Entertainment for Microsoft Windows. It was first released in South Korea on May 3, 2007.

Due to its popularity in Asia, especially China and South Korea, it has become one of the world's most-played video games by player count, with a lifetime total of 1 billion users in 80 countries worldwide. It was the world's top-grossing online game as of 2014, and went on to become one of the highest-grossing video games of all time, having grossed $6.8 billion in lifetime revenue as of 2017.

The game has spawned a media franchise. A film adaptation of the game was announced in October 2015. A Chinese streaming television series based on the game named Crossfire premiered in July 2020 and was a commercial success with more than 1.7 billion views in China as of October 2020. The game was also adapted as part of the animated anthology series Secret Level, released on December 10, 2024. A sequel Crossfire 2 is currently in development.

sources.title: Crossfire (2007 video game) — original release infobox, Wikipedia revision 1373690157

cards.heading: A different route to an audience
cards.text: Smilegate's account of CrossFire begins with a problem. Its Korean service launched in 2007 into a market where other shooters already had established players. The studio needed more than a finished game to find an audience. Working with Tencent, it studied the Chinese market and reached players through QQ messenger. That connection matters: a multiplayer game needs people who can find one another and keep returning. The network around the software became part of the way this Korean-developed shooter reached its Chinese audience.

cards.heading: Build something people return to
cards.text: Smilegate dates the official Chinese service to 2008, a year after the Korean launch. From 2013, CrossFire Stars gave the game its own recurring competition. Teams and spectators gathered around organised tournaments, extending the online service into public events.

cards.heading: Keep the old game in motion
cards.text: In its 2022 results, Tencent described fourteen years of operating CrossFire and highlighted changes to player-versus-environment modes and ranked competition. These updates gave established players new reasons to return and maintained the competitive structure of the PC game.

cards.heading: The same name reaches another device
cards.text: Tencent published CrossFire Mobile, developed by TiMi Studio Group, in 2015. The mobile edition brought the franchise to another audience in China alongside the continuing PC service. Together, the games connected Smilegate's Korean development work with Tencent's publishing network and a separate mobile team.

main.title: Eternal Sonata
main.subtitle: When Music Becomes a Place
main.summary: A role-playing game built around the imagined final moments of composer Fryderyk Chopin.

cards.heading: Chopin's dream and light-based combat
cards.text: tri-Crescendo builds Eternal Sonata around an imagined dream during composer Fryderyk Chopin's final moments. Musical names appear throughout its fantasy world, and light and shadow change the abilities available in combat. Passages about Chopin's life and music sit between sections of the role-playing adventure.

cards.heading: A composer inside a fiction
cards.text: Chopin appears within a fictional world, while separate interludes introduce the historical composer and his music. The game moves between these two forms: a fantasy journey for the party and accounts of the person whose final moments frame it. This structure lets the musical selections receive attention beyond their role as accompaniment.

cards.heading: Fighting in light and shadow
cards.text: Characters use different abilities according to whether they stand in light or shadow. Position matters alongside the time available to act. Battles combine turn-based preparation with direct movement and attacks, asking players to plan where a character should go before carrying out the sequence.

cards.heading: Musical names across the world
cards.text: Musical terms give names to characters and locations throughout the world. These references connect the fantasy setting to the composer without requiring specialist knowledge to follow the adventure. A later PlayStation 3 edition expanded the game beyond its original release.
